title: 1917 USDA Root Cellar Tips
subtitle: Old-Time Wisdom That Still Works
desc: Old-time root cellar tips from USDA Farmers' Bulletin 879, Home Storage of Vegetables (1917), rewritten for today: cool the cellar with outside air on cold nights, shut vents in hard freezes, keep a thermometer inside, hold most root crops at 32–40°F with high humidity, and pull out anything spoiling before it spreads.

title: How to Can Turkey Stock
subtitle: USDA Tested Pressure Method
items: Chill and skim off the fat
desc: How to pressure can leftover Thanksgiving turkey stock, following the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning: simmer the carcass, strain, chill and skim the fat, reheat to boiling, fill hot jars with 1-inch headspace, and process pints 20 minutes or quarts 25 at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–1,000 ft) or 11 lb (dial gauge). Adjust pressure for altitude. Stock must be pressure canned, never water bathed.

title: How to Make Garlic Powder
subtitle: Dehydrate Your Garlic Harvest
desc: How to make homemade garlic powder in a dehydrator or oven: peel and thinly slice garlic, dry at 130–140°F until crisp and brittle, cool, grind and store airtight away from light. A simple way to preserve your garlic harvest. Never store raw garlic in oil at room temperature (botulism risk).

title: Rotate Your Food Storage
subtitle: Keep Your Pantry Fresh
items: Label every jar with a date
New cans go to the back
desc: How to rotate your winter pantry and emergency food storage: use first in, first out, date-label every jar, put new cans at the back, store food in a cool, dry, dark place, discard bulging, leaking or rusted cans, and eat home-canned food within a year for best quality. Self-sufficient living made simple.

title: Build a Simple Cold Frame
subtitle: Grow Greens Into Winter
items: Use an old window as a lid
desc: How to build a simple cold frame to grow vegetables in winter: a south-facing box with a sloped clear lid (an old window works), vented on sunny days so plants don't overheat and closed at night. Keep harvesting cold-hardy spinach, kale and lettuce through late fall and winter. Easy beginner vegetable garden project.
